planting.note: Direct sow an inch deep once the soil has warmed well past last frost, since this bush-type dry bean sulks in cold, wet ground.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep once the soil has warmed well past last frost, since this bush-type dry bean sulks in cold, wet ground. Hopi Black has been grown for generations by Hopi farmers in the arid mesas of northeastern Arizona, selected over centuries for its ability to set a reliable crop of small, glossy black beans on minimal rainfall. Let pods dry fully on the plant before shelling, and expect a compact, drought-tolerant bush that needs no staking. The dried beans cook to a rich, dense texture well suited to stews and traditional Southwestern dishes.

planting.note: Sow seed directly after all frost danger has passed and provide poles, a tepee, or sturdy netting for this vigorous climbing habit.

directions: Sow seed directly after all frost danger has passed and provide poles, a tepee, or sturdy netting for this vigorous climbing habit. Mandan Bride descends from beans grown along the upper Missouri River by the Mandan people, prized as much for its dramatically streaked and mottled seed coat — ranging through maroon, tan, and cream in a single pod — as for its flavor. Keep the vines evenly watered through flowering and podset, then allow pods to dry completely before shelling for storage. It is best treated purely as a dry bean, since pods are fibrous and not suited to snap eating.

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the ground can be worked in late winter, several weeks ahead of the last frost, since this small brown-seeded field pea shrugs off cold snaps.

directions: Direct sow as early as the ground can be worked in late winter, several weeks ahead of the last frost, since this small brown-seeded field pea shrugs off cold snaps. Carlin Pea is a survivor of a once-widespread English tradition of eating dried, soaked, and pan-fried peas on Carlin Sunday in the weeks before Easter, and it remained a staple crop in northern England long after most gardeners moved on to modern shelling peas. Give the vining plants light twiggy brush or netting for support, and either pick pods young for shelling green or let them dry fully on the vine for the traditional parched preparation. The plants tolerate poor soil and are notably resilient compared with modern pea cultivars.

planting.note: Sow directly in cool soil several weeks before the last frost; set stakes, netting, or brush at planting time, as the tall vines will topple without sturdy support.

directions: Sow directly in cool soil several weeks before the last frost, since this tall Victorian heirloom needs a long, cool season to reach its full six-foot height. Introduced in England in 1843, Champion of England quickly became renowned among market gardeners and exhibitors for the exceptionally sweet flavor of its plump pods, a reputation that has kept it in cultivation among heirloom growers ever since. Set stakes, netting, or brush at planting time, as the tall vines will topple without sturdy support. Pick pods regularly once they fill out to keep the vines productive and to catch the peas at their sweetest before starches develop.

planting.note: Direct sow thickly in cool early spring soil; this dwarf Victorian-era heirloom needs no staking and matures quickly.

directions: Direct sow thickly in cool early spring soil; this dwarf Victorian-era heirloom needs no staking and matures quickly, making it one of the earliest garden peas to harvest. Bred in England in the mid-1800s as a compact alternative to the era's towering pea vines, Tom Thumb tops out under a foot tall, which has made it a longtime favorite for small beds, cold frames, and containers. Because the plants are so short, keep them weed-free, as taller neighbors will shade them out quickly. Harvest pods as soon as they plump for the sweetest flavor, since this small-statured variety produces a modest but concentrated crop over a short window.

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following last frost, and set poles or a trellis at planting time, since this semi-climbing French heirloom benefits from support.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following last frost, and set poles or a trellis at planting time, since this semi-climbing French heirloom benefits from support to keep its long pods off the ground. Named for the town of Soissons north of Paris, this large, flat, ivory-white bean has been the traditional centerpiece of French cassoulet for generations, valued for its creamy texture and its ability to hold shape after long, slow cooking. Let pods dry fully on the vine before shelling, then store the beans in a cool, dry place. A single planting yields a substantial harvest of beans well suited to soups, stews, and braises.

planting.note: Sow directly once the soil has warmed after last frost, providing light support such as brush or netting for its semi-climbing habit.

directions: Sow directly once the soil has warmed after last frost, providing light support such as brush or netting for its semi-climbing habit near the cool, damp Brittany coast where it was traditionally grown. Coco de Paimpol earned its own French protected designation for a distinctive fresh-shelling bean — plump, cream-colored seeds lightly speckled with rose, picked while the pods are still green rather than left to fully dry. Harvest pods when the seeds inside have filled out but the pods remain supple, then shell immediately for the tender, buttery texture the variety is prized for. It can also be left to dry fully on the vine for storage as a soup bean, though the fresh-shell stage is when its flavor is best known.
